general.label: GENERAL READER
general.example: Choose one update you have seen recently.
general.simple: Start with the latest update at the top of this page. Open its source and mark one detail you want to understand.
tasks: Read the plain-English summary. Find the exact feature, model, or access change.
Connect the update to a question, task, or decision in your own life.
Try one low-risk example. Do not share private details you would not want stored.
Check the result against a trusted source. Decide whether to use it again.
general.technical: Start at the latest entry. Separate a capability announcement from an availability change, then inspect the source and limits.

sales.label: SALES / BUSINESS DEVELOPMENT
sales.example: Use AI to prepare a relevant first touch.
sales.simple: Pick one public company update. Ask AI for a short account-relevant angle, then verify every fact before sending anything.
tasks: Choose a buyer, account, or industry signal from a cited source.
Ask for a concise opener tied to the prospect’s stated priorities.
Confirm names, facts, permissions, and personalization before sending.
Track reply quality and meetings, not just message volume.
sales.technical: Prototype a sourced account-research and drafting workflow. Gate outbound actions on human review and log source quality, edit rate, reply rate, and meeting conversion.

marketing.label: MARKETING / GROWTH
marketing.example: Turn one release into a small audience test.
marketing.simple: Choose one new feature your audience may care about. Make two clear explainers and see which one helps readers take the next step.
tasks: Choose one segment and one real question they are trying to answer.
Create a beginner version and a practical use-case version.
Check claims, source links, brand voice, privacy, and accessibility.
Compare useful engagement such as saves, completions, and qualified enquiries.
marketing.technical: Build a small content experiment with defined segments, attribution, holdout or baseline, accessible variants, and consent-aware analytics. Optimize qualified outcomes, not vanity clicks.

founder.label: FOUNDER / BUSINESS OWNER
founder.example: Find a repeatable task before buying another tool.
founder.simple: Start with one task that regularly takes your team too long. See whether the AI update helps, then compare the time and quality.
tasks: Name one time-consuming workflow and how often it happens.
Use sample or low-risk data and set a clear success measure.
Count review time, errors, subscription, and data risk as well as speed.
Keep the change, refine it, or stop. Tell the team what you learned.
founder.technical: Frame a narrow pilot with baseline throughput, human review effort, failure thresholds, data classification, model and API costs, and a rollback path.

developer.label: DEVELOPER / IT
developer.example: Turn the release note into a reproducible evaluation.
developer.simple: Try the feature with a small example, then check whether it gives a result you can trust and repeat.
tasks: Check model/API availability, version notes, input limits, and known constraints.
Use test data, scoped credentials, and an observable baseline.
Measure task success, latency, cost, robustness, and human corrections.
Add monitoring, human escalation, rate controls, and a rollback option.
developer.technical: Pin model/version, normalize prompts and fixtures, run representative evaluations, inspect tool permissions, and report quality, latency, cost, and regression deltas before rollout.

operations.label: OPERATIONS / CUSTOMER SUPPORT
operations.example: Reduce one handoff while keeping a human check.
operations.simple: Look for one repeated question or handoff. Let AI prepare a draft, then have a person check it before it reaches a customer.
tasks: Draw the current steps and note where delays, rework, or repeated questions occur.
Let AI summarize or prepare a response while a person still approves it.
Use only approved information. Record mistakes and escalation needs.
Document the new steps and review whether time or resolution quality changed.
operations.technical: Map system boundaries and role access; introduce draft-only automation first, confidence thresholds, exception queues, traceable sources, and service-level/error monitoring.

educator.label: EDUCATOR / TRAINER
educator.example: Turn a feature into a short, checkable lesson.
educator.simple: Ask for a simple demonstration, then compare it with a trusted source and explain the idea in your own words.
tasks: Decide what learners should understand or be able to do.
Use a relevant prompt or visual and make the AI’s role clear.
Review facts, bias, age suitability, accessibility, and privacy.
Invite learners to explain what worked and where human judgment mattered.
educator.technical: Design an outcome-aligned lesson with reproducible prompts, source checks, accessible visuals, privacy boundaries, and an assessment that distinguishes recall from understanding.

student.label: STUDENT / CAREER STARTER
student.example: Use AI to learn a concept, not skip the learning.
student.simple: Ask AI to explain a topic, try a practice question, then check your answer using your course notes or another trusted source.
tasks: Turn one confusing idea into a specific question.
Ask for a hint or a worked example, then solve a similar question on your own.
Review the answer against course materials and note anything uncertain.
Summarize the idea without the tool. Keep track of what you still need to learn.
student.technical: Use the assistant for scaffolding and practice generation; independently solve a parallel task, verify citations, and disclose AI use where your course requires it.

finance: Check the connected source and date
Look for gaps or misclassified items
Verify before any real financial choice
sol: Include price, latency, and review time
pages: Start from material you can share
automation: Use a connected app you can access
Create a draft, not an action
lead: Start with a public, sourced update
Connect it to the account’s stated priorities
support: Review before sending or changing data
